‘You do,’ returned [[characters/arthur|Arthur]]. ‘It has been our cherished purpose.’

‘Very [[motifs/well|well]]!’ said Doyce. ‘Then, if this young lady will do me the [[concepts/honour|honour]]
of regarding me for four-and-twenty hours in the light of a father, and
will take a ride with me now towards Saint Paul’s Churchyard, I dare say
I know what we want to get there.’

Little Dorrit and he went out together soon afterwards, and Mr Meagles
lingered behind to say a word to his friend.

‘I think, [[characters/arthur|Arthur]], you will not want Mother and me in the morning and
we will keep away. It might set Mother thinking about Pet; she’s a
soft-hearted woman. She’s best at the Cottage, and I’ll stay there and
keep her company.’

With that they parted for the [[motifs/time|time]]. And the day ended, and the [[motifs/night|night]]
ended, and the morning came, and Little Dorrit, simply dressed as usual
and having no one with her but Maggy, came into the [[motifs/prison|prison]] with the
sunshine. The poor room was a happy room that morning. Where in the
world was there a room so full of quiet joy!

‘My dear [[motifs/love|love]],’ said [[characters/arthur|Arthur]]. ‘Why does Maggy light the [[motifs/fire|fire]]? We shall be
gone directly.’

‘I asked her to do it. I have taken such an odd fancy. I want you to
burn something for me.’

‘What?’

‘Only this folded paper. If you will put it in the [[motifs/fire|fire]] with your own
hand, just as it is, my fancy will be gratified.’

‘Superstitious, darling Little Dorrit? Is it a charm?’

‘It is anything you like best, my own,’ she answered, laughing with
glistening eyes and standing on tiptoe to kiss him, ‘if you will only
humour me when the [[motifs/fire|fire]] burns up.’

So they stood before the [[motifs/fire|fire]], waiting: Clennam with his arm about her
waist, and the [[motifs/fire|fire]] shining, as [[motifs/fire|fire]] in that same place had often shone,
in Little Dorrit’s eyes. ‘Is it bright enough now?’ said [[characters/arthur|Arthur]]. ‘Quite
bright enough now,’ said Little Dorrit. ‘Does the charm want any words
to be said?’ asked [[characters/arthur|Arthur]], as he held the paper over the flame. ‘You can
say (if you don’t mind) “I [[motifs/love|love]] you!”’ answered Little Dorrit. So he said
it, and the paper burned away.

They passed very quietly along the yard; for no one was there, though
many heads were stealthily peeping from the windows. Only one face,
familiar of old, was in the Lodge. When they had both accosted it, and
spoken many kind words, Little Dorrit turned back one last [[motifs/time|time]] with her
hand stretched out, saying, ‘Good-bye, good John! I [[concepts/hope|hope]] you will live
very happy, dear!’

Then they went up the steps of the neighbouring Saint George’s Church,
and went up to the altar, where [[characters/daniel-doyce|Daniel Doyce]] was waiting in his paternal
character. And there was Little Dorrit’s old friend who had given her
the Burial Register for a pillow; full of admiration that she should
come back to them to be married, after all.

And they were married with the sun shining on them through the painted
figure of Our Saviour on the [[motifs/window|window]]. And they went into the very room
where Little Dorrit had slumbered after her party, to sign the [[motifs/marriage|Marriage]]
Register. And there, [[characters/mr-pancks|Mr Pancks]], (destined to be chief clerk to Doyce and
Clennam, and afterwards partner in the house), sinking the Incendiary
in the peaceful friend, looked in at the door to see it done, with Flora
gallantly supported on one arm and Maggy on the other, and a back-ground
of John Chivery and father and other turnkeys who had run round for the
moment, deserting the parent Marshalsea for its happy [[archetypes/child|child]]. Nor had
Flora the least signs of seclusion upon her, notwithstanding her recent
declaration; but, on the contrary, was wonderfully smart, and enjoyed
the ceremonies mightily, though in a fluttered way.

Little Dorrit’s old friend held the inkstand as she signed her name, and
the clerk paused in taking off the good clergyman’s surplice, and all
the witnesses looked on with special interest. ‘For, you see,’ said
Little Dorrit’s old friend, ‘this young lady is one of our curiosities,
and has come now to the third volume of our Registers. Her birth is in
what I call the first volume; she lay asleep, on this very floor,
with her pretty head on what I call the second volume; and she’s now
a-writing her little name as a bride in what I call the third volume.’

They all gave place when the signing was done, and Little Dorrit and her
husband walked out of the church alone. They paused for a moment on the
steps of the portico, looking at the fresh perspective of the street in
the [[motifs/autumn|autumn]] morning sun’s bright rays, and then went down.

Went down into a modest life of usefulness and happiness. Went down
to give a mother’s care, in the fulness of [[motifs/time|time]], to Fanny’s neglected
children no less than to their own, and to leave that lady going into
Society for ever and a day. Went down to give a tender [[characters/nurse|nurse]] and friend
to Tip for some few years, who was never vexed by the great exactions he
made of her in return for the riches he might have given her if he had
ever had them, and who lovingly closed his eyes upon the Marshalsea
and all its blighted fruits. They went quietly down into the roaring
streets, inseparable and blessed; and as they passed along in sunshine
and shade, the noisy and the eager, and the arrogant and the froward and
the vain, fretted and chafed, and made their usual uproar.

PREFACE TO THE 1857 EDITION


I have been occupied with this story, during many working hours of two
years. I must have been very ill employed, if I could not leave its
merits and demerits as a whole, to express themselves on its being read
as a whole. But, as it is not unreasonable to suppose that I may have
held its threads with a more continuous attention than anyone else can
have given them during its desultory publication, it is not unreasonable
to ask that the weaving may be looked at in its completed state, and
with the pattern finished.

If I might offer any apology for so exaggerated a fiction as the
Barnacles and the Circumlocution Office, I would seek it in the
common experience of an Englishman, without presuming to mention the
unimportant fact of my having done that violence to good manners, in the
days of a Russian war, and of a [[settings/court|Court]] of Inquiry at Chelsea. If I might
make so bold as to defend that extravagant conception, [[characters/mr-merdle|Mr Merdle]], I
would hint that it originated after the Railroad-share epoch, in the
times of a certain Irish bank, and of one or two other equally
laudable enterprises. If I were to plead anything in mitigation of the
preposterous fancy that a bad design will sometimes claim to be a good
and an expressly religious design, it would be the curious coincidence
that it has been brought to its climax in these pages, in the days of
the public examination of late Directors of a Royal British Bank. But,
I submit myself to suffer judgment to go by default on all these counts,
if need be, and to accept the assurance (on good authority) that nothing
like them was ever known in this land.

Some of my readers may have an interest in being informed whether or no
any portions of the Marshalsea [[motifs/prison|Prison]] are yet standing. I did not know,
myself, until the sixth of this present month, when I went to look. I
found the outer front courtyard, often mentioned here, metamorphosed
into a butter shop; and I then almost gave up every brick of the jail
for lost. Wandering, however, down a certain adjacent ‘Angel [[settings/court|Court]],
leading to Bermondsey’, I came to ‘Marshalsea Place:’ the houses in
which I recognised, not only as the great block of the former [[motifs/prison|prison]],
but as preserving the rooms that arose in my mind’s-eye when I became
Little Dorrit’s biographer. The smallest boy I ever conversed with,
carrying the largest baby I ever saw, offered a supernaturally
intelligent explanation of the locality in its old uses, and was very
nearly correct. How this young Newton (for such I judge him to be) came
by his information, I don’t know; he was a quarter of a century too
young to know anything about it of himself. I pointed to the [[motifs/window|window]] of
the room where Little Dorrit was born, and where her father lived so
long, and asked him what was the name of the lodger who tenanted that
apartment at present? He said, ‘Tom Pythick.’ I asked him who was Tom
Pythick? and he said, ‘Joe Pythick’s uncle.’

A little further on, I found the older and smaller wall, which used
to enclose the pent-up inner [[motifs/prison|prison]] where nobody was put, except for
ceremony. But, whosoever goes into Marshalsea Place, turning out of
Angel [[settings/court|Court]], leading to Bermondsey, will find his feet on the very
paving-stones of the extinct Marshalsea jail; will see its narrow yard
to the right and to the left, very little altered if at all, except that
the walls were lowered when the place got free; will look upon rooms
in which the debtors lived; and will stand among the crowding [[motifs/ghosts|ghosts]] of
many miserable years.

In the Preface to Bleak House I remarked that I had never had so many
readers. In the Preface to its next successor, Little Dorrit, I have
still to repeat the same words. Deeply sensible of the affection and
confidence that have grown up between us, I add to this Preface, as I
added to that, May we meet again!

[[settings/london|London]] May 1857

Prefazione all’edizione del 1857


Sono stato impegnato con questa storia per molte ore di lavoro, nel corso di due anni. Devo essere stato davvero mal utilizzato, se non sono riuscito a lasciare che i suoi pregi e i suoi difetti si manifestassero pienamente nella loro interezza, quando veniva letta nel suo insieme. Ma poiché non è irragionevole supporre che io abbia dedicato all’analisi di questa storia un’attenzione più continua di quanto chiunque altro possa averlo fatto durante la sua pubblicazione discontinua, non è nemmeno irragionevole chiedere che l’intero lavoro venga esaminato nella sua forma completa, con il disegno complessivo finalmente realizzato.

Se dovessi chiedere scusa per una finzione così esagerata come “I Barnacles e l’Ufficio delle Circonlocuzioni”, cercherei di giustificarla nell’esperienza comune di un inglese, senza osare menzionare il fatto insignificante che, in tempi di guerra russa e durante un’inchiesta presso la Corte di Chelsea, io abbia trasgredito le regole della buona educazione. Se osassi difendere così audacemente questa concezione stravagante, [[characters/mr-merdle|signor Merdle]], suggerirei che sia nata dopo l’epoca delle azioni ferroviarie, nei tempi di una certa banca irlandese e di un paio di altre imprese altrettanto lodevoli. Se dovessi cercare qualche scusa per questa assurda idea secondo cui un cattivo progetto possa a volte presentarsi come buono, o addirittura come un progetto religioso, sarebbe la curiosa coincidenza che essa abbia raggiunto il suo apice proprio in queste pagine, nei giorni delle indagini pubbliche sui recenti direttori della Royal British Bank. Tuttavia, mi sottometto al giudizio di chiunque, e accetto l’affermazione (fatta da fonti autorevoli) che nulla del genere sia mai stato conosciuto in questo paese.

Alcuni dei miei lettori potrebbero essere interessati a sapere se alcune parti della [[motifs/prison|prigione]] di Marshalsea siano ancora esistenti. Io stesso non lo sapevo fino al sesto giorno di questo mese, quando sono andato a verificare. Ho trovato il cortile anteriore esterno, spesso menzionato in queste pagine, trasformato in un negozio di burro; allora ho quasi pensato che ogni singola pietra della [[motifs/prison|prigione]] fosse andata persa per sempre. Tuttavia, vagando lungo un vicino cortile chiamato “Angel Court”, che conduce a Bermondsey, sono arrivato in Marshalsea Place: le case lì presenti mi sono sembrate non solo il grande complesso dell’ex prigione, ma anche quelle in cui avevo immaginato fossero situate le stanze descritte quando ho iniziato a scrivere la biografia di Little Dorrit. Il bambino più piccolo con cui abbia mai parlato, che portava in braccio il bambino più grande che avessi mai visto, mi ha fornito una spiegazione straordinariamente intelligente riguardo all’uso passato di quegli edifici, e si è quasi sempre dimostrato corretto. Non so come questo giovane “Newton” abbia ottenuto queste informazioni; era troppo giovane per saperne qualcosa di persona. Gli ho indicato la [[motifs/window|finestra]] della stanza in cui Little Dorrit è nata, e dove suo padre aveva vissuto a lungo, e gli ho chiesto come si chiamasse l’inquilino attuale di quell’appartamento. Lui ha risposto: “Tom Pythick”. Gli ho chiesto chi fosse Tom Pythick, e lui ha detto: “Lo zio di Joe Pythick”.

Un po’ più avanti, trovai il muro più vecchio e più basso che un tempo circondava quella [[motifs/prison|prigione]] interna in cui nessuno veniva rinchiuso, se non per scopi cerimoniali. Ma chiunque entri in Marshalsea Place, uscendo da Angel Court e proseguendo verso Bermondsey, si troverà sui medesimi ciottoli della defunta prigione di Marshalsea; vedrà il suo cortile stretto, a destra e a sinistra, quasi del tutto intatto, se non per il fatto che i muri sono stati abbassati quando quel luogo è stato liberato; vedrà le stanze in cui vivevano i debitori. E si troverà circondato dai “[[motifs/ghosts|fantasmi]]” di molti anni tragici.

Nella prefazione a *Bleak House*, ho osservato di non aver mai avuto così tanti lettori. Nella prefazione al suo successore, *Little Dorrit*, devo ancora ripetere le stesse parole. Consapevole profondamente dell'affetto e della fiducia che si sono sviluppati tra noi, aggiungo a questa prefazione, come ho fatto all’altra: Possiamo incontrarci di nuovo!

[[settings/london|Londra]], maggio 1857



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_03_sun_and_shadow--part_01" data-title="Little Dorrit — Chapter 1: Sun and [[Shadow (part 1)" data-chapter="Sun and Shadow" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/king,archetype/shadow,motif/bells,motif/dust,motif/fire,motif/hill,motif/jewel,motif/leaves,motif/night,motif/prison,motif/river,motif/road,motif/time,motif/water,motif/well,motif/wind,motif/window,character/bottom"></span>


BOOK THE FIRST: [[concepts/poverty|POVERTY]]
CHAPTER 1. Sun and [[archetypes/shadow|Shadow]]


Thirty years ago, Marseilles lay burning in the sun, one day.

A blazing sun upon a fierce August day was no greater rarity in southern
France then, than at any other [[motifs/time|time]], before or since. Everything in
Marseilles, and about Marseilles, had stared at the fervid sky, and been
stared at in return, until a staring habit had become universal there.
Strangers were stared out of countenance by staring white houses,
staring white walls, staring white streets, staring tracts of arid [[motifs/road|road]],
staring hills from which verdure was burnt away. The only things to be
seen not fixedly staring and glaring were the vines drooping under their
load of grapes. These did occasionally wink a little, as the hot air
barely moved their faint [[motifs/leaves|leaves]].

There was no [[motifs/wind|wind]] to make a ripple on the foul [[motifs/water|water]] within the harbour,
or on the beautiful sea without. The line of demarcation between the two
colours, black and blue, showed the point which the pure sea would not
pass; but it lay as quiet as the abominable pool, with which it never
mixed. Boats without awnings were too hot to touch; ships blistered at
their moorings; the stones of the quays had not cooled, [[motifs/night|night]] or
day, for months. Hindoos, Russians, Chinese, Spaniards, Portuguese,
Englishmen, Frenchmen, Genoese, Neapolitans, Venetians, Greeks, Turks,
descendants from all the builders of Babel, come to trade at Marseilles,
sought the shade alike--taking refuge in any hiding-place from a sea too
intensely blue to be looked at, and a sky of purple, set with one great
flaming [[motifs/jewel|jewel]] of [[motifs/fire|fire]].

The universal stare made the eyes ache. Towards the distant line of
Italian coast, indeed, it was a little relieved by light clouds of mist,
slowly rising from the evaporation of the sea, but it softened nowhere
else. Far away the staring roads, deep in [[motifs/dust|dust]], stared from the
[[motifs/hill|hill]]-side, stared from the hollow, stared from the interminable
plain. Far away the dusty vines overhanging wayside cottages, and the
monotonous wayside avenues of parched trees without shade, drooped
beneath the stare of earth and sky. So did the horses with drowsy [[motifs/bells|bells]],
in long files of carts, creeping slowly towards the interior; so did
their recumbent drivers, when they were awake, which rarely happened;
so did the exhausted labourers in the fields. Everything that lived or
grew, was oppressed by the glare; except the lizard, passing swiftly
over rough stone walls, and the cicala, chirping his dry hot chirp, like
a rattle. The very [[motifs/dust|dust]] was scorched brown, and something quivered in
the atmosphere as if the air itself were panting.

Blinds, shutters, curtains, awnings, were all closed and drawn to keep
out the stare. Grant it but a chink or keyhole, and it shot in like a
white-hot arrow. The churches were the freest from it. To come out of
the twilight of pillars and arches--dreamily dotted with winking lamps,
dreamily peopled with ugly old shadows piously dozing, spitting, and
begging--was to plunge into a fiery [[motifs/river|river]], and swim for life to the
nearest strip of shade. So, with people lounging and lying wherever
shade was, with but little hum of tongues or barking of dogs, with
occasional jangling of discordant church [[motifs/bells|bells]] and rattling of vicious
drums, Marseilles, a fact to be strongly smelt and tasted, lay broiling
in the sun one day.

In Marseilles that day there was a villainous [[motifs/prison|prison]]. In one of its
chambers, so repulsive a place that even the obtrusive stare blinked at
it, and left it to such refuse of reflected light as it could find for
itself, were two men. Besides the two men, a notched and disfigured
bench, immovable from the wall, with a draught-board rudely hacked upon
it with a knife, a set of draughts, made of old buttons and soup bones,
a set of dominoes, two mats, and two or three wine bottles. That was all
the chamber held, exclusive of rats and other unseen vermin, in addition
to the seen vermin, the two men.

It received such light as it got through a grating of iron bars
fashioned like a pretty large [[motifs/window|window]], by means of which it could be
always inspected from the gloomy staircase on which the grating gave.
There was a broad strong ledge of stone to this grating where the [[characters/bottom|bottom]]
of it was let into the masonry, three or four feet above the ground.
Upon it, one of the two men lolled, half sitting and half lying, with
his knees drawn up, and his feet and shoulders planted against the
opposite sides of the aperture. The bars were wide enough apart to
admit of his thrusting his arm through to the elbow; and so he held on
negligently, for his greater ease.

A [[motifs/prison|prison]] taint was on everything there. The imprisoned air, the
imprisoned light, the imprisoned damps, the imprisoned men, were all
deteriorated by confinement. As the captive men were faded and haggard,
so the iron was rusty, the stone was slimy, the wood was rotten, the air
was faint, the light was dim. Like a [[motifs/well|well]], like a vault, like a tomb,
the [[motifs/prison|prison]] had no knowledge of the brightness outside, and would have
kept its polluted atmosphere intact in one of the spice islands of the
Indian ocean.

The man who lay on the ledge of the grating was even chilled. He jerked
his great cloak more heavily upon him by an impatient movement of one
shoulder, and growled, ‘To the devil with this Brigand of a Sun that
never shines in here!’

He was waiting to be fed, looking sideways through the bars that he
might see the further down the stairs, with much of the expression of
a wild beast in similar expectation. But his eyes, too close together,
were not so nobly set in his head as those of the [[archetypes/king|king]] of beasts are in
his, and they were sharp rather than bright--pointed weapons with little
surface to betray them. They had no depth or change; they glittered,
and they opened and shut. So far, and waiving their use to himself, a
clockmaker could have made a better pair. He had a hook nose, handsome
after its kind, but too high between the eyes by probably just as much
as his eyes were too near to one another. For the rest, he was large and
tall in frame, had thin lips, where his thick moustache showed them at
all, and a quantity of dry hair, of no definable colour, in its shaggy
state, but shot with red. The hand with which he held the grating
(seamed all over the back with ugly scratches newly healed), was
unusually small and plump; would have been unusually white but for the
[[motifs/prison|prison]] grime.


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

LIBRO PRIMO: [[concepts/poverty|Povertà]]
CAPITOLO 1. Sole e [[archetypes/shadow|>Ombra]]


Trent’anni fa, un giorno, Marsiglia bruciava sotto il sole.

Un sole ardente in una torrida giornata di agosto non era affatto una rarità nel sud della Francia, né prima né dopo. Tutto a Marsiglia, e nei dintorni di Marsiglia, fissava quel cielo infuocato; anche il cielo, a sua volta, sembrava fissare tutto quanto. Gli sconosciuti venivano osservati con insistenza da case bianche, muri bianchi, strade bianche, distese aride di [[motifs/road|strada]], colline dalle quali ogni traccia di verde era scomparsa. Le uniche cose che non fissavano nulla erano le viti, piegate sotto il peso dei grappoli. Di tanto in tanto, quelle viti sembravano “socchiudere” leggermente i loro deboli [[motifs/leaves|fogli]] quando l’aria calda li muoveva appena.

Non c'era alcun [[motifs/wind|>vento]] che potesse creare increspature sull'orribile [[motifs/water|acqua]] del porto, né sul bellissimo mare al di fuori di esso. Il confine tra i due colori, il nero e il blu, indicava il punto oltre cui l'acqua pura non avrebbe mai potuto spingersi; tuttavia, rimaneva immobile, proprio come quell’orribile stagno con cui mai si mescolava. Le barche senza tetto erano troppo calde da toccare; le navi si scottavano dove erano ancorate; le pietre dei moli non si erano raffreddate, né di [[motifs/night|notte]] né di giorno, da mesi. Indù, russi, cinesi, spagnoli, portoghesi, inglesi, francesi, genovesi, napoletani, veneziani, greci, turchi, discendenti di tutti coloro che avevano costruito Babilonia, venivano a Marsiglia per fare affari e cercavano tutti lo stesso riparo: un luogo nascosto dove sfuggire a quel mare troppo intensamente blu da poter essere guardato, e a quel cielo viola, adornato da un enorme [[motifs/jewel|>jewello]] di [[motifs/fire|fuoco]].

Quel bagliore uniforme faceva male agli occhi. Verso la lontana linea della costa italiana, infatti, il cielo era un po’ alleviato da leggere nuvole di nebbia che si alzavano lentamente a causa dell’evaporazione del mare, ma altrove quel bagliore non si attenuava affatto. Lontano, le strade polverose, immerse nella [[motifs/dust|polvere]], sembravano fissare il paesaggio da ogni lato: dalle pendici delle [[motifs/hill|colline]], dalle valli, dalle sterminate pianure. Anche i viticci polverosi che si estendevano lungo le case ai bordi della strada, e le monotone alberate prive di ombra, sembravano sottomessi a quel bagliore incessante. Lo stesso valeva per i cavalli con i loro sonnolenti [[motifs/bells|campanelli]], per le lunghe file di carri che avanzavano lentamente verso l’interno del paese; lo stesso valeva per i conducenti, quando erano svegli, il che accadeva raramente; e anche per gli stanchi lavoratori nei campi. Tutto ciò che viveva o cresceva era oppresso da quel bagliore accecante, tranne la lucertola che si muoveva rapidamente sopra le pareti di pietra ruvida, e il cuculo che emetteva il suo canto secco e caldo, simile al suono di un sonaglio. Anche la stessa [[motifs/dust|polvere]] era diventata di colore marrone scuro; qualcosa tremolava nell’atmosfera, come se l’aria stessa fosse in affanno.

Persiane, scuri, tende e tettoie erano tutte chiuse per tenere fuori quegli sguardi invadenti. Bastava una fessura o un buco della serratura, e quegli sguardi si riversavano dentro come frecce incandescenti. Le chiese, invece, erano le uniche a esserne al riparo. Uscire dall’oscurità creata da colonne e archi – illuminati solo da lampade che lampeggiavano dolcemente, popolati da ombre vecchie e brutte che dormivano, sputavano e chiedevano l’elemosina – significava tuffarsi in un [[motifs/river|fiume]] di fuoco e nuotare disperatamente verso la prima ombra disponibile. Così, mentre le persone si sdraiavano ovunque ci fosse ombra, con pochissimo rumore di voci o abbai di cani, e solo di tanto in tanto il suono discordante delle [[motifs/bells|campane]] delle chiese o il rimbombo dei tamburi minacciosi. Marsiglia, una realtà da percepire con tutti i sensi, ardeva sotto il sole quel giorno.

Quel giorno a Marsiglia c'era una malvagia [[motifs/prison|prigione]]. In una delle sue stanze, un luogo così ripugnante che persino lo sguardo più insistente faticava a sostenerlo, e che riceveva soltanto quella luce riflessa che riusciva a captare da solo, c'erano due uomini. Oltre a loro, c'era una panca incavata e deformata, fissata al muro; su di essa era stato rudemente costruito un tavolo da dama con dei bottoni vecchi e delle ossa di zuppa; inoltre, c'erano delle carte da domino, due tappeti e due o tre bottiglie di vino. Quello era tutto ciò che conteneva la stanza, a parte i ratti e altri insetti invisibili, e, naturalmente, i due uomini stessi.

Riceveva quella luce perché passava attraverso una grata di sbarre di ferro, disposta a forma di una piuttosto grande [[motifs/window|finestra]], grazie alla quale era possibile controllarla in qualsiasi momento dal buio corridoio su cui si trovava la grata stessa. C’era un largo e solido bordo in pietra sotto quella grata; la sua parte inferiore era infatti inserita nella muratura, a tre o quattro piedi di altezza dal suolo. Su quel bordo, uno dei due uomini si appoggiava, seduto a metà e sdraiato a metà, con le ginocchia raccolte e i piedi e le spalle premuti contro i lati opposti dell’apertura. Le sbarre erano abbastanza distanziate tra loro da permettergli di infilare il braccio fino al gomito; così si teneva appoggiato, con noncuranza, per maggiore comodità.

In quella [[motifs/prison|prigione]] tutto era contaminato. L’aria imprigionata, la luce imprigionata, l’umidità imprigionata, gli uomini imprigionati, tutto era deteriorato a causa della reclusione. Proprio come gli uomini erano pallidi e smunti, così anche il ferro si arrugginiva, la pietra diventava viscosa, il legno marciva, l’aria diventava rarefatta, la luce fioca. Come una [[motifs/well|prigione sotterranea]], come un sepolcro, quella [[motifs/prison|prigione]] non conosceva affatto la luce esterna e avrebbe mantenuto la sua atmosfera inquinata intatta, proprio come una delle isole profumate dell’Oceano Indiano.

L’uomo sdraiato sul bordo della grata era persino intirritato dal freddo. Con un movimento impaziente di una spalla, si avvolse più strettamente nel suo grande mantello e borbottò: “Al diavolo questo ‘brigante di sole’ che mai splende qui dentro!”

Aspettava di essere nutrito, guardando di sottecchi attraverso le sbarre, nella speranza di vedere qualcosa più in basso sulle scale. Con un’espressione simile a quella di una bestia selvatica in attesa della sua preda. Ma i suoi occhi, troppo vicini tra loro, non erano così “nobilmente” posizionati nel suo viso come quelli del [[archetypes/king|re]] delle bestie; erano acuti, ma non luminosi. Sembravano armi affilate, prive di qualsiasi traccia di espressività. Non avevano profondità né variazioni nell’aspetto; brillavano semplicemente, aprendosi e chiudendosi continuamente. Un orologiaio avrebbe potuto costruire una coppia di occhi migliori. Aveva il naso adunco, attraente per la sua forma, ma troppo alto tra gli occhi. E questi ultimi erano troppo vicini tra loro. Per il resto, era di statura alta e robusta; aveva labbra sottili, e solo il suo folto mustacchio le rendeva visibili; i suoi capelli erano secchi, di colore indefinito e arruffati. E qua e là spuntavano ciocche rosse. La mano con cui teneva la grata – coperta di brutte cicatrici appena guarite – era insolitamente piccola e rotonda; sarebbe stata bianca, se non fosse stata imbrattata dalla sporcizia della [[motifs/prison|prigione]].



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_03_sun_and_shadow--part_02" data-title="Little Dorrit — Chapter 1: Sun and [[Shadow (part 2)" data-chapter="Sun and Shadow" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/child,motif/bells,motif/birds,motif/city,motif/clock,motif/night,motif/prison,motif/rose,motif/sleep,motif/time,motif/well,concept/grotesque,character/rigaud"></span>


The other man was lying on the stone floor, covered with a coarse brown
coat.

‘Get up, pig!’ growled the first. ‘Don’t [[motifs/sleep|sleep]] when I am hungry.’

‘It’s all one, master,’ said the pig, in a submissive manner, and not
without cheerfulness; ‘I can wake when I will, I can [[motifs/sleep|sleep]] when I will.
It’s all the same.’

As he said it, he [[motifs/rose|rose]], shook himself, scratched himself, tied his brown
coat loosely round his neck by the sleeves (he had previously used it
as a coverlet), and sat down upon the pavement yawning, with his back
against the wall opposite to the grating.

‘Say what the hour is,’ grumbled the first man.

‘The mid-day [[motifs/bells|bells]] will ring--in forty minutes.’ When he made the
little pause, he had looked round the [[motifs/prison|prison]]-room, as if for certain
information.

‘You are a [[motifs/clock|clock]]. How is it that you always know?’

‘How can I say? I always know what the hour is, and where I am. I was
brought in here at [[motifs/night|night]], and out of a boat, but I know where I am. See
here! Marseilles harbour;’ on his knees on the pavement, mapping it all
out with a swarthy forefinger; ‘Toulon (where the galleys are), Spain
over there, Algiers over _there_. Creeping away to the left here, Nice.
Round by the Cornice to Genoa. Genoa Mole and Harbour. Quarantine
Ground. [[motifs/city|City]] there; terrace gardens blushing with the bella donna. Here,
Porto Fino. Stand out for Leghorn. Out again for Civita Vecchia, so away
to--hey! there’s no room for Naples;’ he had got to the wall by this
[[motifs/time|time]]; ‘but it’s all one; it’s in there!’

He remained on his knees, looking up at his fellow-prisoner with a
lively look for a [[motifs/prison|prison]]. A sunburnt, quick, lithe, little man, though
rather thickset. Earrings in his brown ears, white teeth lighting up his
[[concepts/grotesque|grotesque]] brown face, intensely black hair clustering about his brown
throat, a ragged red shirt open at his brown breast. Loose, seaman-like
trousers, decent shoes, a long red cap, a red sash round his waist, and
a knife in it.

‘Judge if I come back from Naples as I went! See here, my master! Civita
Vecchia, Leghorn, Porto Fino, Genoa, Cornice, Off Nice (which is in
there), Marseilles, you and me. The apartment of the jailer and his keys
is where I put this thumb; and here at my wrist they keep the national
razor in its case--the guillotine locked up.’

The other man spat suddenly on the pavement, and gurgled in his throat.

Some lock below gurgled in _its_ throat immediately afterwards, and then
a door crashed. Slow steps began ascending the stairs; the prattle of
a sweet little voice mingled with the noise they made; and the
[[motifs/prison|prison]]-keeper appeared carrying his daughter, three or four years old,
and a basket.

‘How goes the world this forenoon, gentlemen? My little one, you see,
going round with me to have a peep at her father’s [[motifs/birds|birds]]. Fie, then!
Look at the [[motifs/birds|birds]], my pretty, look at the [[motifs/birds|birds]].’

He looked sharply at the [[motifs/birds|birds]] himself, as he held the [[archetypes/child|child]] up at
the grate, especially at the little bird, whose activity he seemed to
mistrust. ‘I have brought your bread, Signor John Baptist,’ said he
(they all spoke in French, but the little man was an Italian); ‘and if I
might recommend you not to game--’

‘You don’t recommend the master!’ said John Baptist, showing his teeth
as he smiled.

‘Oh! but the master wins,’ returned the jailer, with a passing look of
no particular liking at the other man, ‘and you lose. It’s quite another
thing. You get husky bread and sour drink by it; and he gets sausage of
Lyons, veal in savoury jelly, white bread, strachino cheese, and good
wine by it. Look at the [[motifs/birds|birds]], my pretty!’

‘Poor [[motifs/birds|birds]]!’ said the [[archetypes/child|child]].

The fair little face, touched with divine compassion, as it peeped
shrinkingly through the grate, was like an angel’s in the [[motifs/prison|prison]]. John
Baptist [[motifs/rose|rose]] and moved towards it, as if it had a good attraction for
him. The other bird remained as before, except for an impatient glance
at the basket.

‘Stay!’ said the jailer, putting his little daughter on the outer ledge
of the grate, ‘she shall feed the [[motifs/birds|birds]]. This big loaf is for Signor
John Baptist. We must break it to get it through into the cage. So,
there’s a tame bird to kiss the little hand! This sausage in a vine
leaf is for Monsieur [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]]. Again--this veal in savoury jelly is for
Monsieur [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]]. Again--these three white little loaves are for Monsieur
[[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]]. Again, this cheese--again, this wine--again, this tobacco--all
for Monsieur [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]]. Lucky bird!’

The [[archetypes/child|child]] put all these things between the bars into the soft, Smooth,
[[motifs/well|well]]-shaped hand, with evident dread--more than once drawing back
her own and looking at the man with her fair brow roughened into an
expression half of fright and half of anger. Whereas she had put the
lump of coarse bread into the swart, scaled, knotted hands of John
Baptist (who had scarcely as much nail on his eight fingers and two
thumbs as would have made out one for Monsieur [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]]), with ready
confidence; and, when he kissed her hand, had herself passed it
caressingly over his face. Monsieur [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]], indifferent to this
distinction, propitiated the father by laughing and nodding at the
daughter as often as she gave him anything; and, so soon as he had
all his viands about him in convenient nooks of the ledge on which he
rested, began to eat with an appetite.

When Monsieur [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]] laughed, a change took place in his face, that
was more remarkable than prepossessing. His moustache went up under his
nose, and his nose came down over his moustache, in a very sinister and
cruel manner.

‘There!’ said the jailer, turning his basket upside down to beat the
crumbs out, ‘I have expended all the money I received; here is the note
of it, and _that’s_ a thing accomplished. Monsieur [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]], as I expected
yesterday, the President will look for the pleasure of your society at
an hour after mid-day, to-day.’


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

L’altro uomo giaceva sul pavimento di pietra, coperto da un ruvido cappotto marrone.

“Alzati, maiale!” ringhiò il primo. “Non [[motifs/sleep|)dormire]] quando ho fame.”

“È tutto lo stesso, padrone,” disse il maiale in tono sottomesso, e non senza allegria; “Posso svegliarmi quando voglio, posso [[motifs/sleep|)dormire]] quando voglio. È davvero la stessa cosa.”

Non appena lo ebbe detto, si alzò in piedi, si scosse, si grattò, legò strettamente il suo cappotto marrone intorno al collo passandolo attraverso le maniche (prima lo aveva usato come coperta) e si sedette sul marciapiede sbadigliando, appoggiato al muro di fronte alla grata.

“Dimmi che ora è,” borbottò il primo uomo.

“I campanelli di mezzogiorno suoneranno tra quaranta minuti.” Mentre faceva quella breve pausa, aveva guardato intorno nella stanza della prigione, come se cercasse informazioni precise.

“Sei un’[[motifs/clock|orologio]]. Come fai sempre a saperlo?”

“Come posso dirlo? So sempre che ora è e dove mi trovo. Sono stato portato qui di [[motifs/night|notte]], da una barca, ma so esattamente dove sono. Guardate! Il porto di Marsiglia, ” Si mise in ginocchio sul marciapiede e indicò con il dito indice tutte le località: “Tolone, la Spagna laggiù. Algeri ancora più lontano. A sinistra c’è Nizza. Lungo la Costa Azzurra fino a Genova. Il Molo di Genova e il suo porto. Qui, Porto Fino. Più avanti c’è Livorno. E poi Civita Vecchia, ” Arrivato al muro, aggiunse: “Ma in fondo è tutto parte dello stesso insieme. È tutto lì dentro!”

Rimase in ginocchio, alzando lo sguardo verso il suo compagno di prigione con un'espressione vivace, all'interno di una [[motifs/prison|prigione]]. Un ometto abbronzato, agile e snello, sebbene piuttosto robusto. Orecchini alle orecchie marroni; denti bianchi che risaltavano sul suo viso marrone, un po’ “grottesco”; capelli neri folti intorno al collo marrone; una camicia rossa stracciata aperta sul petto marrone. Pantaloni larghi, da marinaio; scarpe decenti; un lungo berretto rosso; una cintura rossa intorno alla vita. E dentro di essa, un coltello.

‘Giudicate se tornerò da Napoli come sono partito! Ecco qui, mio padrone: Civita Vecchia, Livorno, Porto Fino, Genova, la Costa Azzurra, Off Nice (che si trova lì), Marsiglia. L’appartamento del carceriere e le sue chiavi. È lì che ho nascosto il pollice; e qui al mio polso tengono la rasoietta nazionale nella sua custodia. La ghigliottina è chiusa a chiave.’

L’altro uomo sputò improvvisamente sul marciapiede e cominciò a gracchiare.

Subito dopo, qualche chiave sotto di lui iniziò a gorgogliare nel suo “gorlo”, e poi una porta si aprì con violenza. Passi lenti iniziarono ad salire le scale; il chiacchiericcio di una dolce vocina infantile si mescolò al rumore che facevano; e il custode della [[motifs/prison|prigione]] apparve, portando con sé sua figlia, di tre o quattro anni, e un cestino.

“Come va il mondo questa mattina, signori? Mia piccola, vedete,
sta venendo con me a dare un’occhiata agli uccelli di suo padre. Che meraviglia!
Guardate gli uccellini, mia cara, guardateli bene.”

Guardò attentamente gli [[motifs/birds|uccelli]] stesso, tenendo il [[archetypes/child|bambino]] vicino alla grata, soprattutto quel piccolo uccellino, la cui attività sembrava non fidarsi del tutto. “Ho portato il vostro pane, Signor Giovanni Battista,” disse (tutti parlavano francese, ma quell’uomo era italiano); “e se potessi consigliarvi di non cacciare, ”

“Non raccomandi quel maestro!” disse Giovanni Battista, mostrando i denti mentre sorrideva.

“Oh! Ma il padrone vince,” rispose il carceriere, lanciando un’occhiata al altro uomo che non sembrava particolarmente gradire; “e tu perdi. È tutta un’altra cosa: tu ottieni solo pane secco e bevande acide; mentre lui riceve salsiccia di Lione, vitello in gelatina saporita, pane bianco, formaggio strachino e buon vino. Guarda quelle [[motifs/birds|uccelline]], mia bella, ”

“Poveri [[motifs/birds|uccelli]]!” disse il [[archetypes/child|bambino]].

Quel bel visino, toccato da una divina compassione, mentre spuntava timidamente attraverso la grata, sembrava quello di un angelo in quella [[motifs/prison|prigione]]. Giovanni Battista si [[motifs/rose|alzò]] e si avvicinò a esso, come se fosse attratto da qualcosa di positivo. L’altro uccello rimase fermo al suo posto, tranne per uno sguardo impaziente verso il cestino.

“Resta qui!” disse il carceriere, mettendo sua figlia sulla ringhiera esterna della gabbia. “Lei potrà dare da mangiare agli [[motifs/birds|uccelli]]. Questo grande pane è per il Signor Giovanni Battista; dobbiamo spezzarlo per farlo passare dentro la gabbia. Ecco, c’è anche un uccello addomesticato che può baciare la manina della bambina! Questa salsiccia avvolta in una foglia di vite è per il Signor [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]]; quest’altra carne di vitella in gelatina è sempre per lui. E questi tre piccoli pani bianchi, e anche questo formaggio, questo vino, questo tabacco, tutto per il Signor [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]]. Che fortuna per quell’uccello, ”

La [[archetypes/child|>bambina]], con evidente timore, mise tutte queste cose tra le sbarre e le portò nella sua mano morbida, liscia e ben formata; più di una volta ritrasse la propria mano e guardò l’uomo, con la fronte pallida corrugata in un’espressione a metà paura e a metà rabbia. Mentre invece aveva messo il pezzo di pane ruvido nelle mani nere, squamose e nodose di John Baptist (che aveva appena abbastanza unghie sui suoi otto dita e due pollici per farne una sola per Monsieur [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]]), con grande fiducia; e quando lui le baciò la mano, lei stessa la passò dolcemente sul suo viso. Monsieur [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]], indifferente a questa differenza, compiacque il padre ridendo e annuendo ogni volta che la figlia gli dava qualcosa; e non appena ebbe tutti i suoi cibi disposti in posti comodi sulla roccia su cui si riposava, iniziò a mangiare con grande appetito.

Quando Monsieur [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]] rideva, il suo viso subiva un cambiamento che era più notevole che attraente. I suoi mustacchi si sollevavano sotto il naso, e il naso si abbassava sopra i mustacchi, in modo molto sinistro e crudele.

“Eccola!” disse il carceriere, capovolgendo il cesto per far cadere le briciole, “Ho speso tutto il denaro che ho ricevuto; ecco la ricevuta, e questa è davvero una cosa fatta. Monsieur [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]], come mi aspettavo ieri, il Presidente desidera godere della vostra compagnia tra un’ora dopo mezzogiorno di oggi.”



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_03_sun_and_shadow--part_03" data-title="Little Dorrit — Chapter 1: Sun and [[Shadow (part 3)" data-chapter="Sun and Shadow" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/child,archetype/innocent,archetype/king,motif/birds,motif/death,motif/leaves,motif/night,motif/prison,motif/road,motif/time,motif/water,motif/window,concept/honour,concept/imprisonment,character/rigaud"></span>


‘To try me, eh?’ said [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]], pausing, knife in hand and morsel in
mouth.

‘You have said it. To try you.’

‘There is no news for me?’ asked John Baptist, who had begun,
contentedly, to munch his bread.

The jailer shrugged his shoulders.

‘Lady of mine! Am I to lie here all my life, my father?’

‘What do I know!’ cried the jailer, turning upon him with southern
quickness, and gesticulating with both his hands and all his fingers,
as if he were threatening to tear him to pieces. ‘My friend, how is it
possible for me to tell how long you are to lie here? What do I know,
John Baptist Cavalletto? [[motifs/death|Death]] of my life! There are prisoners here
sometimes, who are not in such a devil of a hurry to be tried.’

He seemed to glance obliquely at Monsieur [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]] in this remark; but
Monsieur [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]] had already resumed his meal, though not with quite so
quick an appetite as before.

‘Adieu, my [[motifs/birds|birds]]!’ said the keeper of the [[motifs/prison|prison]], taking his pretty
[[archetypes/child|child]] in his arms, and dictating the words with a kiss.

‘Adieu, my [[motifs/birds|birds]]!’ the pretty [[archetypes/child|child]] repeated.

Her [[archetypes/innocent|innocent]] face looked back so brightly over his shoulder, as he
walked away with her, singing her the song of the [[archetypes/child|child]]’s game:

‘Who passes by this [[motifs/road|road]] so late?
Compagnon de la Majolaine!
Who passes by this [[motifs/road|road]] so late?
Always gay!’

that John Baptist felt it a point of [[concepts/honour|honour]] to reply at the grate, and
in good [[motifs/time|time]] and tune, though a little hoarsely:

‘Of all the [[archetypes/king|king]]’s knights ‘tis the flower,
Compagnon de la Majolaine!
Of all the [[archetypes/king|king]]’s knights ‘tis the flower,
Always gay!’

Which accompanied them so far down the few steep stairs, that the
[[motifs/prison|prison]]-keeper had to stop at last for his little daughter to hear the
song out, and repeat the Refrain while they were yet in sight. Then the
[[archetypes/child|child]]’s head disappeared, and the [[motifs/prison|prison]]-keeper’s head disappeared, but
the little voice prolonged the strain until the door clashed.

Monsieur [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]], finding the listening John Baptist in his way before
the echoes had ceased (even the echoes were the weaker for [[concepts/imprisonment|imprisonment]],
and seemed to lag), reminded him with a push of his foot that he had
better resume his own darker place. The little man sat down again
upon the pavement with the negligent ease of one who was thoroughly
accustomed to pavements; and placing three hunks of coarse bread before
himself, and falling to upon a fourth, began contentedly to work his way
through them as if to clear them off were a sort of game.

Perhaps he glanced at the Lyons sausage, and perhaps he glanced at the
veal in savoury jelly, but they were not there long, to make his mouth
[[motifs/water|water]]; Monsieur [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]] soon dispatched them, in spite of the president
and tribunal, and proceeded to suck his fingers as clean as he could,
and to wipe them on his vine [[motifs/leaves|leaves]]. Then, as he paused in his drink
to contemplate his fellow-prisoner, his moustache went up, and his nose
came down.

‘How do you find the bread?’

‘A little dry, but I have my old sauce here,’ returned John Baptist,
holding up his knife.

‘How sauce?’

‘I can cut my bread so--like a melon. Or so--like an omelette. Or
so--like a fried fish. Or so--like Lyons sausage,’ said John Baptist,
demonstrating the various cuts on the bread he held, and soberly chewing
what he had in his mouth.

‘Here!’ cried Monsieur [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]]. ‘You may drink. You may finish this.’

It was no great gift, for there was mighty little wine left; but Signor
Cavalletto, jumping to his feet, received the bottle gratefully, turned
it upside down at his mouth, and smacked his lips.

‘Put the bottle by with the rest,’ said [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]].

The little man obeyed his orders, and stood ready to give him a lighted
match; for he was now rolling his tobacco into cigarettes by the aid of
little squares of paper which had been brought in with it.

‘Here! You may have one.’

‘A thousand thanks, my master!’ John Baptist said in his own language,
and with the quick conciliatory manner of his own countrymen.

Monsieur [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]] arose, lighted a cigarette, put the rest of his stock
into a breast-pocket, and stretched himself out at full length upon the
bench. Cavalletto sat down on the pavement, holding one of his ankles in
each hand, and smoking peacefully. There seemed to be some uncomfortable
attraction of Monsieur [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]]’s eyes to the immediate neighbourhood of
that part of the pavement where the thumb had been in the plan. They
were so drawn in that direction, that the Italian more than once
followed them to and back from the pavement in some surprise.

‘What an infernal hole this is!’ said Monsieur [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]], breaking a long
pause. ‘Look at the light of day. Day? the light of yesterday week, the
light of six months ago, the light of six years ago. So slack and dead!’

It came languishing down a square funnel that blinded a [[motifs/window|window]] in the
staircase wall, through which the sky was never seen--nor anything else.

‘Cavalletto,’ said Monsieur [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]], suddenly withdrawing his gaze from
this funnel to which they had both involuntarily turned their eyes, ‘you
know me for a gentleman?’

‘Surely, surely!’

‘How long have we been here?’

‘I, eleven weeks, to-morrow [[motifs/night|night]] at midnight. You, nine weeks and three
days, at five this afternoon.’

‘Have I ever done anything here? Ever touched the broom, or spread
the mats, or rolled them up, or found the draughts, or collected the
dominoes, or put my hand to any kind of work?’

‘Never!’

‘Have you ever thought of looking to me to do any kind of work?’

John Baptist answered with that peculiar back-handed shake of the
right forefinger which is the most expressive negative in the Italian
language.

‘No! You knew from the first moment when you saw me here, that I was a
gentleman?’


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

“Per mettermi alla prova, eh?”, disse [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]], fermandosi per un attimo, con il coltello in mano e un boccone in bocca.

“L’hai detto tu stesso. Per metterti alla prova.”

“Non ci sono nuove per me?”, chiese Giovanni Battista, che aveva iniziato a masticare felicemente il suo pane.

Il carceriere alzò le spalle.

“Mia signora. Devo rimanere sdraiato qui per tutta la vita, padre mio?”

“Cosa ne so io!” gridò il carceriere, girandosi verso di lui con la rapidità tipica del Sud e gesticolando con entrambe le mani e tutti i dita, come se volesse strapparlo in pezzi. “Amico mio, come potrei mai sapere per quanto tempo dovrai rimanere qui? Cosa ne so io, John Baptist Cavalletto. Mio Dio! A volte ci sono prigionieri qui che non hanno affatto fretta di essere processati.”

Sembrava che, con quel commento, gettasse uno sguardo obliquo verso Monsieur [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]]; ma Monsieur [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]] aveva già ripreso a mangiare, sebbene non con lo stesso appetito di prima.

“Addio, miei [[motifs/birds|uccelli]]!” disse il custode della [[motifs/prison|prigione]], prendendo in braccio la sua bella [[archetypes/child|bambina]] e pronunciando quelle parole mentre le baciava.

“Addio, miei [[motifs/birds|uccellini]]!” ripeté la bella >bambina.

Il suo viso [[archetypes/innocent|innocente]] lo guardava ancora con tanta dolcezza mentre lui si allontanava cantandole la canzone del gioco dei bambini.

“Chi passa per questa [[motifs/road|strada]] a quest’ora tarda?  
Compagno di Majolaine!  
Chi passa per questa [[motifs/road|strada]] a quest’ora tarda?  
Sempre allegro!”

Che Giovanni Battista ritenesse un dovere di [[concepts/honour|onore]] rispondere attraverso la grata, e farlo nel giusto [[motifs/time|tempo]] e con la giusta melodia, anche se con una voce un po' roca.

“Di tutti i cavalieri del [[archetypes/king|re]], è proprio lui il fiore,
Compagno di Majolaine!
Di tutti i cavalieri del [[archetypes/king|re]], è proprio lui il fiore,
Sempre gioioso!”

Che li accompagnò per tutta la lunghezza di quei pochi gradini ripidi, fino a quando il custode della [[motifs/prison|prigione]] dovette fermarsi, affinché sua figlia potesse sentire fino in fondo quella cantata e ripetere il ritornello mentre erano ancora visibili. Poi la testa del piccolo scomparve, e anche la testa del custode della [[motifs/prison|prigione]] scomparve; ma quella vocina continuò a cantare fino a quando la porta non si chiuse.

Monsieur [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]], trovando John Baptist ad ascoltare proprio davanti a sé prima che gli echi si fossero spenti (anche gli echi, a causa dell’[[concepts/imprisonment|prigionia]], erano più deboli e sembravano ritardare nel propagarsi), lo spinse con il piede per ricordargli di tornare al proprio “oscuro posto”. Il piccolo uomo si sedette di nuovo sul marciapiede con quella noncurante disinvoltura tipica di chi è completamente abituato a vivere in mezzo ai marciapiedi; posizionò davanti a sé tre pezzi di pane grezzo e, prendendo un quarto, iniziò felicemente a mangiarli, come se pulirli fosse una sorta di gioco.

Forse gettò un’occhiata alla salsiccia Lyons, e forse anche alla vitella in gelatina aromatica, ma non rimasero a lungo lì, tanto da fargli venire l’acquolina in bocca. Monsieur [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]] le eliminò rapidamente, nonostante la presenza del presidente e del tribunale, poi si pulì le dita il più accuratamente possibile e se le asciugò sulle foglie di vite. Poi, mentre si fermava a bere per osservare il suo compagno di prigione, i suoi mustacchi si sollevarono e il suo naso si abbassò.

Come si trova il pane?

“Un po’ secco, ma ho qui il mio vecchio condimento,” rispose Giovanni Battista, alzando il suo coltello.

“Che tipo di salsa?”

“Posso tagliare il mio pane in modo che assomigli a una melona. O a un omelette. O a un pesce fritto. O anche a una salsiccia di Lyons,” disse Giovanni Battista, mostrando i vari modi in cui poteva tagliare il pane che teneva in mano e masticando con calma ciò che aveva in bocca.

“Ecco!” gridò il signor [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]]. “Puoi bere. Puoi finirlo tutto.”

Non era certo un regalo eccezionale, poiché era rimasto molto poco vino; ma il signor Cavalletto, alzandosi in piedi di scatto, accettò la bottiglia con gratitudine, la capovolse davanti alla bocca e si leccò le labbra.

“Metti la bottiglia insieme alle altre,” disse [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]].

Quel piccolo uomo obbedì ai suoi ordini e si preparò ad offrirgli un fiammifero acceso; infatti, in quel momento stava arrotolando il tabacco per farne delle sigarette, utilizzando dei piccoli quadratini di carta che aveva portato con sé.

“Ecco! Puoi prenderne uno.”

“Mille grazie, mio padrone!” disse Giovanni Battista nella sua lingua nativa, con quel modo rapido e accomodante tipico dei suoi connazionali.

Monsieur [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]] si alzò, accese una sigaretta, mise il resto del suo tabacco in una tasca del petto e si sdraiò completamente sul banco. Cavalletto si sedette sul marciapiede, tenendo ciascun polso attorno a uno dei propri talloni e fumando tranquillamente. Sembrava che lo sguardo di Monsieur [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]] fosse attratto in modo particolare dalla zona del marciapiede dove il pollice si trovava nel disegno. Lo sguardo era così fisso in quella direzione che l’italiano, più volte, lo seguì con sorpresa mentre si spostava avanti e indietro lungo il marciapiede.

“Che inferno è questo posto!” disse il signor [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]] dopo una lunga pausa. “Guardate questa luce. La luce del giorno? Ma è la luce di settimane fa, di sei mesi fa, di sei anni fa. Debole e spenta, ”

Scendeva lentamente lungo un tubo quadrato che oscurava una [[motifs/window|finestra]] nel muro della scala; da quella finestra non si vedeva mai il cielo, né nulla altro.

“Cavalletto,” disse Monsieur [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]], distogliendo improvvisamente lo sguardo da quel imbuto verso cui entrambi avevano involontariamente rivolto gli occhi, “mi conosci come un gentiluomo, vero?”

“Certamente, certamente!”

“Da quanto tempo siamo qui?”

“Io, undici settimane, domani [[motifs/night|notte]] a mezzanotte. Tu, nove settimane e tre giorni, alle cinque di questo pomeriggio.”

“Ho mai fatto qualcosa qui? Ho mai usato la scopa, ho mai steso o arrotolato i tappeti, ho mai cercato le fessure d’aria, ho mai raccolto i dadi da domino, o ho mai svolto qualsiasi tipo di lavoro?”

“Mai!”

“Hai mai pensato di chiedermi di aiutarti con qualche lavoro?”

Giovanni Battista rispose con quel particolare gesto negativo fatto scuotendo il dito indice destro, che rappresenta l’espressione di rifiuto più efficace nella lingua italiana.

“No! Dal primo momento in cui mi hai visto qui, sapevi già che ero un gentiluomo, ”



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_03_sun_and_shadow--part_04" data-title="Little Dorrit — Chapter 1: Sun and [[Shadow (part 4)" data-chapter="Sun and Shadow" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/blood,motif/cross,motif/soul,motif/well,concept/beauty,concept/hope,concept/pride,character/rigaud"></span>


‘ALTRO!’ returned John Baptist, closing his eyes and giving his head a
most vehement toss. The word being, according to its Genoese emphasis,
a confirmation, a contradiction, an assertion, a denial, a taunt,
a compliment, a joke, and fifty other things, became in the present
instance, with a significance beyond all power of written expression,
our familiar English ‘I believe you!’

‘Haha! You are right! A gentleman I am! And a gentleman I’ll live, and
a gentleman I’ll die! It’s my intent to be a gentleman. It’s my game.
[[motifs/death|Death]] of my [[motifs/soul|soul]], I play it out wherever I go!’

He changed his posture to a sitting one, crying with a triumphant air:

‘Here I am! See me! Shaken out of destiny’s dice-box into the company
of a mere smuggler;--shut up with a poor little contraband trader, whose
papers are wrong, and whom the police lay hold of besides, for placing
his boat (as a means of getting beyond the frontier) at the disposition
of other little people whose papers are wrong; and he instinctively
recognises my position, even by this light and in this place. It’s [[motifs/well|well]]
done! By Heaven! I win, however the game goes.’

Again his moustache went up, and his nose came down.

‘What’s the hour now?’ he asked, with a dry hot pallor upon him, rather
difficult of association with merriment.

‘A little half-hour after mid-day.’

‘Good! The President will have a gentleman before him soon. Come!
Shall I tell you on what accusation? It must be now, or never, for I
shall not return here. Either I shall go free, or I shall go to be made
ready for shaving. You know where they keep the razor.’

Signor Cavalletto took his cigarette from between his parted lips, and
showed more momentary discomfiture than might have been expected.

‘I am a’--Monsieur [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]] stood up to say it--‘I am a cosmopolitan
gentleman. I own no particular country. My father was Swiss--Canton de
Vaud. My mother was French by [[motifs/blood|blood]], English by birth. I myself was born
in Belgium. I am a citizen of the world.’

His theatrical air, as he stood with one arm on his hip within the folds
of his cloak, together with his manner of disregarding his companion
and addressing the opposite wall instead, seemed to intimate that he
was rehearsing for the President, whose examination he was shortly to
undergo, rather than troubling himself merely to enlighten so small a
person as John Baptist Cavalletto.

‘Call me five-and-thirty years of age. I have seen the world. I have
lived here, and lived there, and lived like a gentleman everywhere. I
have been treated and respected as a gentleman universally. If you try
to prejudice me by making out that I have lived by my wits--how do
your lawyers live--your politicians--your intriguers--your men of the
Exchange?’

He kept his small smooth hand in constant requisition, as if it were a
witness to his gentility that had often done him good service before.

‘Two years ago I came to Marseilles. I admit that I was poor; I had been
ill. When your lawyers, your politicians, your intriguers, your men of
the Exchange fall ill, and have not scraped money together, _they_ become
poor. I put up at the [[motifs/cross|Cross]] of Gold,--kept then by Monsieur Henri
Barronneau--sixty-five at least, and in a failing state of health. I had
lived in the house some four months when Monsieur Henri Barronneau had
the misfortune to die;--at any rate, not a rare misfortune, that. It
happens without any aid of mine, pretty often.’

John Baptist having smoked his cigarette down to his fingers’ ends,
Monsieur [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]] had the magnanimity to throw him another. He lighted the
second at the ashes of the first, and smoked on, looking sideways at his
companion, who, preoccupied with his own case, hardly looked at him.

‘Monsieur Barronneau left a widow. She was two-and-twenty. She had
gained a reputation for [[concepts/beauty|beauty]], and (which is often another thing) was
beautiful. I continued to live at the [[motifs/cross|Cross]] of Gold. I married Madame
Barronneau. It is not for me to say whether there was any great
disparity in such a match. Here I stand, with the contamination of a
jail upon me; but it is possible that you may think me better suited to
her than her former husband was.’

He had a certain air of being a handsome man--which he was not; and
a certain air of being a [[motifs/well|well]]-bred man--which he was not. It was mere
swagger and challenge; but in this particular, as in many others,
blustering assertion goes for proof, half over the world.

‘Be it as it may, Madame Barronneau approved of me. _That_ is not to
prejudice me, I [[concepts/hope|hope]]?’

His eye happening to light upon John Baptist with this inquiry, that
little man briskly shook his head in the negative, and repeated in an
argumentative tone under his breath, altro, altro, altro, altro--an
infinite number of times.

‘Now came the difficulties of our position. I am proud. I say nothing
in defence of [[concepts/pride|pride]], but I am proud. It is also my character to govern.
I can’t submit; I must govern. Unfortunately, the property of Madame
[[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]] was settled upon herself. Such was the insane act of her late
husband. More unfortunately still, she had relations. When a wife’s
relations interpose against a husband who is a gentleman, who is proud,
and who must govern, the consequences are inimical to peace. There
was yet another source of difference between us. Madame [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]] was
unfortunately a little vulgar. I sought to improve her manners and
ameliorate her general tone; she (supported in this likewise by her
relations) resented my endeavours. Quarrels began to arise between us;
and, propagated and exaggerated by the slanders of the relations of
Madame [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]], to become notorious to the neighbours. It has been said
that I treated Madame [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]] with cruelty. I may have been seen to slap
her face--nothing more. I have a light hand; and if I have been seen
apparently to correct Madame [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]] in that manner, I have done it
almost playfully.’

If the playfulness of Monsieur [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]] were at all expressed by his smile
at this point, the relations of Madame [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]] might have said that
they would have much preferred his correcting that unfortunate woman
seriously.


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

“Altro!”, rispose Giovanni Battista, chiudendo gli occhi e scuotendo violentemente la testa. Quella parola, secondo l’accento genovese con cui veniva pronunciata, poteva significare conferma, contraddizione, affermazione, negazione, scherno, complimento, battuta, o qualunque altra cosa. In quel momento, però, assunse un significato che andava oltre qualsiasi espressione scritta; era l’equivalente del nostro familiare “Credo a te!”.

‘Ahah! Hai ragione! Sono un gentiluomo. E lo sarò per tutta la vita, e lo sarò anche quando morirò. È il mio obiettivo essere un gentiluomo. È il mio “gioco”. Anche di fronte alla [[motifs/death|Morte]] della mia [[motifs/soul|'anima]], continuerò a comportarmi da gentiluomo, ovunque io vada!’

Si sistemò in posizione seduta, piangendo con un’espressione trionfale.

‘Eccomi qui! Guardatemi. Sono stato strappato dalla “scatola dei dadi del destino” per finire nella compagnia di un semplice contrabbandiere; costretto a collaborare con un povero commerciante di merci illegali, il cui passaporto è falso, e che inoltre viene arrestato dalla polizia perché permette ad altre persone, anch’esse con documenti falsi, di utilizzare la sua barca per attraversare il confine. Lui intuisce immediatamente la mia situazione, anche in queste condizioni e in questo luogo. [[motifs/well|Bene]] fatto! Per Dio. Vinco, qualunque sia l’esito della partita.’

Di nuovo, la sua barba si sollevò e il suo naso si abbassò.

“Che ore sono adesso?”, chiese, con un pallore giallastro e secco sul viso; un aspetto che difficilmente poteva essere associato alla gioia.

“Un quarto d’ora dopo mezzogiorno.”

‘Bene! Presto il Presidente avrà davanti a sé un gentiluomo. Vieni! Devo dirti con quale accusa? Deve essere ora, o mai più, perché non tornerò qui. O uscirò libero, oppure andrò a farmi preparare per la rasatura. Sai dove tengono il rasoio.’

Il signor Cavalletto prese la sigaretta tra le labbra divaricate e mostrò un certo imbarazzo momentaneo, più di quanto ci si sarebbe aspettati.

“Sono un, ” – Monsieur [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]] si alzò per dirlo – “sono un gentiluomo cosmopolita. Non appartengo a nessun paese in particolare. Mio padre era svizzero, del Cantone di Vaud; mia madre era di [[motifs/blood|origine]] francese, ma inglese di nascita. Io stesso sono nato in Belgio. Sono un cittadino del mondo.”

Il suo atteggiamento teatrale, mentre stava lì con un braccio appoggiato alla vita all’interno delle pieghe del suo mantello, unito al modo in cui ignorava il suo compagno e si rivolgeva invece al muro di fronte, sembravano indicare che stesse provando per l’interrogatorio che avrebbe presto dovuto affrontare con il Presidente, piuttosto che preoccuparsi semplicemente di illuminare una persona così insignificante come John Baptist Cavalletto.

“Chiamatemi un uomo di cinquantatré anni: ho visto il mondo, ho vissuto qui e lì, e ovunque mi sono comportato da gentiluomo. Sono stato trattato e rispettato come tale in ogni luogo. Se cercate di danneggiarmi sostenendo che mi sia guadagnato da vivere con l’inganno, come fanno a vivere i vostri avvocati, i vostri politici, i vostri intrighisti, gli uomini del mercato finanziario?”

Teneva sempre la sua piccola mano liscia a disposizione, come se fosse una testimonianza della sua gentilezza, che in passato gli aveva spesso reso dei grandi servizi.

“Due anni fa sono arrivato a Marsiglia. Ammetto di essere stato povero; ero malato. Quando i vostri avvocati, i vostri politici, i vostri intrighanti, gli uomini del mercato finanziario si ammalano e non riescono a raccogliere abbastanza denaro, _loro_ diventano poveri. Io soggiornavo all’[[motifs/cross|Crocce d’Oro]] – gestito all’epoca da Monsieur Henri Barronneau – da almeno sessantacinque giorni, e in uno stato di salute precario. Ero già vissuto in quella casa per circa quattro mesi quando Monsieur Henri Barronneau ebbe la sfortuna di morire. Comunque, non si trattava certo di una sfortuna rara. Queste cose accadono spesso, senza alcun mio intervento.”

Dopo aver fumato la sigaretta fino a che le punte delle dita non erano diventate rosse, Monsieur [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]] ebbe la magnanimità di offrirgliene un’altra. Accese la seconda con le ceneri della prima e continuò a fumare, guardando di sottecchi il suo compagno, che, assorto nei propri pensieri, quasi non gli prestava attenzione.

‘Monsieur Barronneau lasciò una vedova. Aveva ventidue anni. Era conosciuta per la sua [[concepts/beauty|bellezza]], e, beh, era davvero bella. Continuai a vivere alla [[motifs/cross|>Croce d’Oro]]. Sposai Madame Barronneau. Non spetta a me giudicare se ci fosse una grande disparità in un matrimonio del genere. Ora mi trovo qui, con il “peso” di aver trascorso del tempo in prigione; ma forse voi penserete che io sia più adatto a lei di quanto lo fosse suo ex marito.’

Aveva quell'aspetto tipico di un uomo attraente, ma non lo era affatto; e anche quell’aria di essere un uomo ben educato, ma non lo era nemmeno. Era solo una questione di atteggiamento e sfida; ma in questo, come in molti altri casi, le affermazioni prepotenti vengono spesso scambiate per prove, in molte parti del mondo.

“Comunque sia, Madame Barronneau mi ha approvato. _Questo_ non dovrebbe danneggiarmi, spero, ”

Il suo sguardo si posò su Giovanni Battista con questa domanda; quell’uomo piccolo scosse rapidamente la testa in segno di negazione e ripeté, con tono argomentativo e a bassa voce, “altro, altro, altro, altro, ” – un numero infinito di volte.

‘Ora arrivarono le difficoltà legate alla nostra situazione. Sono orgoglioso. Non dico nulla a difesa dell’[[concepts/pride|orgoglio]], ma sono orgoglioso. È anche nel mio carattere governare: non posso sottomettermi, devo governare. Purtroppo, i beni di Madame [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]] le furono lasciati in eredità. Fu un atto folle da parte del suo defunto marito. Ancora più sfortunatamente, lei aveva delle relazioni. Quando le relazioni di una moglie si oppongono a un marito che è un gentiluomo, orgoglioso e deciso a governare, le conseguenze sono dannose per la pace. C’era anche un altro motivo di dissidio tra noi: Madame [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]] era, purtroppo, piuttosto volgare. Cercai di migliorare i suoi modi e il suo comportamento generale; lei, appoggiata anch’essa dalle sue relazioni, osteggiò i miei sforzi. Iniziarono a sorgere litigi tra noi. E questi litigi, amplificati e esagerati dalle calunnie delle relazioni di Madame [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]], divennero noti in tutto il quartiere. Si è detto che trattassi Madame [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]] con crudeltà. Forse qualcuno mi ha visto schiaffiarla. Nient’altro. Ho una mano leggera; e se qualcuno mi ha visto correggerla in quel modo, l’ho fatto quasi per scherzo.’

Se la spensieratezza di Monsieur [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]] fosse stata in qualche modo evidente dal suo sorriso in quel momento, le relazioni tra Madame [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]] e lui avrebbero potuto indicare che lei avrebbe preferito molto se lui avesse corretto seriamente quella sfortunata donna.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_03_sun_and_shadow--part_05" data-title="Little Dorrit — Chapter 1: Sun and [[Shadow (part 5)" data-chapter="Sun and Shadow" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/death,motif/dust,motif/fire,motif/leaves,motif/love,motif/night,motif/prison,motif/silence,motif/sleep,motif/stars,motif/storm,motif/time,motif/well,concept/doubt,concept/freedom,concept/grotesque,concept/history,form/history,character/rigaud"></span>


‘I am sensitive and brave. I do not advance it as a merit to be
sensitive and brave, but it is my character. If the male relations of
Madame [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]] had put themselves forward openly, I should have known how
to deal with them. They knew that, and their machinations were conducted
in secret; consequently, Madame [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]] and I were brought into frequent
and unfortunate collision. Even when I wanted any little sum of money
for my personal expenses, I could not obtain it without collision--and
I, too, a man whose character it is to govern! One [[motifs/night|night]], Madame [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]]
and myself were walking amicably--I may say like lovers--on a height
overhanging the sea. An evil star occasioned Madame [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]] to advert to
her relations; I reasoned with her on that subject, and remonstrated on
the want of duty and devotion manifested in her allowing herself to be
influenced by their jealous animosity towards her husband. Madame [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]]
retorted; I retorted; Madame [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]] grew warm; I grew warm, and provoked
her. I admit it. Frankness is a part of my character. At length, Madame
[[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]], in an access of fury that I must ever deplore, threw herself
upon me with screams of passion (no [[concepts/doubt|doubt]] those that were overheard
at some distance), tore my clothes, tore my hair, lacerated my hands,
trampled and trod the [[motifs/dust|dust]], and finally leaped over, dashing herself to
[[motifs/death|death]] upon the rocks below. Such is the train of incidents which
malice has perverted into my endeavouring to force from Madame [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]]
a relinquishment of her rights; and, on her persistence in a refusal to
make the concession I required, struggling with her--assassinating her!’

He stepped aside to the ledge where the vine [[motifs/leaves|leaves]] yet lay strewn
about, collected two or three, and stood wiping his hands upon them,
with his back to the light.

‘[[motifs/well|Well]],’ he demanded after a [[motifs/silence|silence]], ‘have you nothing to say to all
that?’

‘It’s ugly,’ returned the little man, who had risen, and was brightening
his knife upon his shoe, as he leaned an arm against the wall.

‘What do you mean?’

John Baptist polished his knife in [[motifs/silence|silence]].

‘Do you mean that I have not represented the case correctly?’

‘Al-tro!’ returned John Baptist. The word was an apology now, and stood
for ‘Oh, by no means!’

‘What then?’

‘Presidents and tribunals are so prejudiced.’

‘[[motifs/well|Well]],’ cried the other, uneasily flinging the end of his cloak over his
shoulder with an oath, ‘let them do their worst!’

‘Truly I think they will,’ murmured John Baptist to himself, as he bent
his head to put his knife in his sash.

Nothing more was said on either side, though they both began walking
to and fro, and necessarily crossed at every turn. Monsieur [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]]
sometimes stopped, as if he were going to put his case in a new light,
or make some irate remonstrance; but Signor Cavalletto continuing to
go slowly to and fro at a [[concepts/grotesque|grotesque]] kind of jog-trot pace with his eyes
turned downward, nothing came of these inclinings.

By-and-by the noise of the key in the lock arrested them both. The sound
of voices succeeded, and the tread of feet. The door clashed, the voices
and the feet came on, and the [[motifs/prison|prison]]-keeper slowly ascended the stairs,
followed by a guard of soldiers.

‘Now, Monsieur [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]],’ said he, pausing for a moment at the grate, with
his keys in his hands, ‘have the goodness to come out.’

‘I am to depart in state, I see?’

‘Why, unless you did,’ returned the jailer, ‘you might depart in so many
pieces that it would be difficult to get you together again. There’s a
crowd, Monsieur [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]], and it doesn’t [[motifs/love|love]] you.’

He passed on out of sight, and unlocked and unbarred a low door in the
corner of the chamber. ‘Now,’ said he, as he opened it and appeared
within, ‘come out.’

There is no sort of whiteness in all the hues under the sun at all like
the whiteness of Monsieur [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]]’s face as it was then. Neither is there
any expression of the human countenance at all like that expression in
every little line of which the frightened heart is seen to beat. Both
are conventionally compared with [[motifs/death|death]]; but the difference is the whole
deep gulf between the struggle done, and the fight at its most desperate
extremity.

He lighted another of his paper cigars at his companion’s; put it
tightly between his teeth; covered his head with a soft slouched hat;
threw the end of his cloak over his shoulder again; and walked out into
the side gallery on which the door opened, without taking any further
notice of Signor Cavalletto. As to that little man himself, his whole
attention had become absorbed in getting near the door and looking out
at it. Precisely as a beast might approach the opened gate of his den
and eye the [[concepts/freedom|freedom]] beyond, he passed those few moments in watching and
peering, until the door was closed upon him.

There was an officer in command of the soldiers; a stout, serviceable,
profoundly calm man, with his drawn sword in his hand, smoking a cigar.
He very briefly directed the placing of Monsieur [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]] in the midst of
the party, put himself with consummate indifference at their head, gave
the word ‘march!’ and so they all went jingling down the staircase. The
door clashed--the key turned--and a ray of unusual light, and a breath
of unusual air, seemed to have passed through the jail, vanishing in a
tiny wreath of smoke from the cigar.

Still, in his captivity, like a lower animal--like some impatient ape,
or roused bear of the smaller species--the prisoner, now left solitary,
had jumped upon the ledge, to lose no glimpse of this departure. As he
yet stood clasping the grate with both hands, an uproar broke upon his
hearing; yells, shrieks, oaths, threats, execrations, all comprehended
in it, though (as in a [[motifs/storm|storm]]) nothing but a raging swell of sound
distinctly heard.

Excited into a still greater resemblance to a caged wild animal by his
anxiety to know more, the prisoner leaped nimbly down, ran round the
chamber, leaped nimbly up again, clasped the grate and tried to shake
it, leaped down and ran, leaped up and listened, and never rested until
the noise, becoming more and more distant, had died away. How many
better prisoners have worn their noble hearts out so; no man thinking
of it; not even the beloved of their souls realising it; great kings
and governors, who had made them captive, careering in the sunlight
jauntily, and men cheering them on. Even the said great personages dying
in bed, making exemplary ends and sounding speeches; and polite [[concepts/history|history]],
more servile than their instruments, embalming them!

At last, John Baptist, now able to choose his own spot within the
compass of those walls for the exercise of his faculty of going to [[motifs/sleep|sleep]]
when he would, lay down upon the bench, with his face turned over on his
crossed arms, and slumbered. In his submission, in his lightness, in his
good humour, in his short-lived passion, in his easy contentment with
hard bread and hard stones, in his ready [[motifs/sleep|sleep]], in his fits and starts,
altogether a true son of the land that gave him birth.

The wide stare stared itself out for one while; the Sun went down in
a red, green, golden glory; the [[motifs/stars|stars]] came out in the heavens, and the
[[motifs/fire|fire]]-flies mimicked them in the lower air, as men may feebly imitate
the goodness of a better order of beings; the long dusty roads and the
interminable plains were in repose--and so deep a hush was on the sea,
that it scarcely whispered of the [[motifs/time|time]] when it shall give up its dead.


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

“Sono sensibile e coraggioso. Non lo presento come un merito, ma è semplicemente il mio carattere. Se le relazioni maschili di Madame [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]] si fossero fatte avanti apertamente, avrei saputo come affrontarle. Loro lo sapevano, e le loro macchinazioni venivano condotte in segreto; di conseguenza, Madame [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]] ed io ci scontravamo spesso e in modo spiacevole. Anche quando volevo chiedere una piccola somma di denaro per le mie spese personali, non riuscivo a ottenerla senza conflitti. E io, che sono un uomo il cui carattere consiste nel governare con equità! Una [[motifs/night|notte]], Madame [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]] ed io camminavamo amichevolmente – potrei dire come innamorati su una collina che si affacciava sul mare. Per un motivo crudele, Madame Rigaud iniziò a parlare delle sue relazioni; ne discutemmo, e le feci notare quanto fosse mancante di dovere e devozione nel lasciarsi influenzare dall’invidia e dall’ostilità di quelle persone verso suo marito. Madame [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]] ribatté; io risposi; lei si arrabbiò ancora di più; anch’io mi infervorii, provocandola. Lo ammetto: la franchezza fa parte del mio carattere. Alla fine, Madame [[characters/rigaud|Rigaud]], presa da un attacco di furia che deploro profondamente, si gettò su di me urlando di passione (non c’è dubbio che qualcuno abbia sentito quelle grida da lontano), strappò i miei vestiti, i miei capelli, mi ferì le mani, calpestò il terreno, e infine si gettò giù dalle rocce, morendo.
